stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The musicologist Hedda Lindqvist, whose decade-long survey of Scandinavian herding calls drew on more than four hundred field recordings made between 1952 and ______ that the calls were never simply signals to cattle. Many of them, she showed, carried coded messages meant for other herders working on distant slopes.
explanation: The comma after "Lindqvist" opens a long relative clause ("whose decade-long survey... between 1952 and 1971") that adds removable information about her. You need a matching comma to close it before the main verb "argued." If you cross out the interrupter, you get "The musicologist Hedda Lindqvist argued that the calls were never simply signals," which is a complete, correct sentence.

A.why: You left the interrupter open. The comma after "Lindqvist" starts the relative clause, and without a closing comma the clause runs straight into "argued," so the sentence no longer shows where the extra information ends and the main clause picks up again.

B.why: You added "and" as if two verbs were being joined. There is no earlier main verb for "argued" to pair with. The subject "Lindqvist" has no verb of its own until "argued," so "and" breaks the sentence.

D.why: A semicolon has to separate two complete sentences. Everything before it is a subject plus a modifier with no main verb, which is a fragment, so a semicolon can't go there.

rated_why: Subtle comma usage for coordinating verbs; 'and argued' and bare 'argued' both superficially defensible

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Meteorologists reviewing radar images of the storm complex that crossed the northern plains last July noticed that its leading edge had stayed intact far longer than usual. The system—a derecho whose gust front advanced more than 900 kilometers in under eleven ______ later classified as the most damaging windstorm in the region's recorded history.
explanation: The dash after "system" opens an interruption that describes the storm. An interruption opened with a dash has to close with a dash. Cross it out and you get "The system was later classified as the most damaging windstorm," which is correct. Only the closing dash completes the pair.

A.why: You closed the interruption with a different mark than the one that opened it. A dash and a comma can't form a pair, so the interruption stays unclosed.

B.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. "The system—a derecho... eleven hours" has no main verb, so it's a fragment and can't come before a semicolon.

C.why: You left the interruption open. Without a closing dash, the descriptive phrase runs straight into "was," and nothing marks where the extra information ends and the main clause resumes.

subtype_name: Close the interrupter: match the opening comma

rated_why: Em dash punctuation for interrupted appositive is less familiar; comma, semicolon, and dash all compete

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Regulatory T cells, a small population of white blood cells first distinguished in the mid-1990s by their unusually high expression ______ keep the immune system from attacking the body's own tissues. When these cells are depleted in laboratory mice, the animals rapidly develop autoimmune disease.
choices: of the protein CD25, and help
explanation: The comma after "Regulatory T cells" opens an appositive that describes the cells, and the appositive ends after "CD25." A single closing comma goes there, before the main verb "help," and no punctuation goes inside the phrase. With the appositive removed, you get "Regulatory T cells help keep the immune system from attacking the body's own tissues."

A.why: You put a comma inside the phrase. "Expression of the protein CD25" is one unit, and a comma between the preposition "of" and its object splits it at a point where no punctuation belongs.

C.why: You left the appositive open. The comma after "cells" needs a partner after "CD25," or the descriptive phrase runs straight into the main verb "help."

D.why: You added "and" as if two actions were being joined. The subject "Regulatory T cells" has no verb before this point, so "and help" has nothing to join, and the sentence has no main verb.

rated_why: Complex comma placement in nested structure with prepositional phrase; multiple commas test precision

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In the early 1800s the French weaver Joseph-Marie Jacquard introduced a loom attachment that, by reading a long chain of punched ______ a single operator weave intricate brocades. Such patterns had once required a second worker, perched above the loom, to lift each warp thread by hand.
choices: cards laced together in sequence let
cards, laced together in sequence let
cards laced together in sequence, and let
cards laced together in sequence, let
explanation: The comma after "that" opens the phrase "by reading a long chain of punched cards laced together in sequence," which explains how the attachment worked. The phrase has to close with a comma before "let," the verb of the "that" clause. With the phrase removed, you get "a loom attachment that let a single operator weave intricate brocades," which is correct.

A.why: You left the interrupter open. The comma after "that" has no closing partner, so the "by reading..." phrase runs straight into "let."

B.why: You closed the interrupter too early, in the middle of it. "Cards laced together in sequence" is one noun phrase, and the comma after "cards" cuts it apart. That leaves "laced together in sequence let" as a jumble with no clear grammatical role.

C.why: You added "and" as if two verbs were being joined. The "that" clause has no verb before "let," so "and" has nothing to join, and the clause loses its verb.

adjudication.why: The comma after "that" opens the phrase "by reading... in sequence," so a second comma must close it before the verb "let"; A leaves it unclosed.

rated_why: Participial phrase comma placement plus coordination; 'and let' tempts as explicit coordination

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When the colonial survey of the coast began in 1868, its chief draftsman, a former naval officer who had charted harbors in Chile, Peru, and ______ that every stretch of shoreline be redrawn from fresh depth soundings rather than copied from older Spanish charts.
explanation: The comma after "draftsman" opens an appositive describing him, and that appositive contains a list of its own. The commas in "Chile, Peru, and" belong to the list and don't close anything. The appositive ends after "Ecuador," so a comma goes there before the main verb "insisted." With the appositive removed, you get "its chief draftsman insisted that every stretch of shoreline be redrawn."

A.why: You took one of the list commas as the closing comma and left the appositive open. The comma after "draftsman" still needs its partner after "Ecuador."

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. The text before it has a subject, "draftsman," but no main verb, so it's a fragment.

D.why: You added "and" as if two things were being joined. Here "and" could only extend the list of countries, but "insisted" is the draftsman's main verb, not another place he charted.

stimulus: Barcelona's superblocks—clusters of nine city blocks within which through traffic is rerouted to the surrounding perimeter ______ converted dozens of former intersections into plazas, playgrounds, and shaded seating areas. Planners in several other European cities are now studying the model to see whether it could be adapted to their own street grids.
explanation: The dash after "superblocks" opens an interruption that defines the term. An interruption opened with a dash must close with a dash, so one goes after "streets." With the interruption removed, you get "Barcelona's superblocks have converted dozens of former intersections into plazas," which is a complete, correct sentence.

A.why: You closed with a different mark than the one that opened the interruption. A dash can't be paired with a comma, so the interruption stays open.

B.why: You left the interruption open. Nothing marks where the definition ends and the main verb "have" begins.

D.why: The closing dash is right, but you added "and" as if two verbs were being joined. "Superblocks" has no verb before "have," so "and" has nothing to join, and the sentence loses its main verb.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Before setting out on a nonstop flight of more than 11,000 kilometers from Alaska to New Zealand, a journey first documented through satellite ______ roughly doubles its body mass by storing fat. At the same time, several of its digestive organs shrink, reducing the weight the bird must carry.
explanation: The sentence opens with a long introductory phrase, "Before setting out... satellite tracking," and inside it an appositive ("a journey first documented through satellite tracking") is set off by the comma after "New Zealand." A single comma after "tracking" closes the appositive and ends the introductory phrase where it hands off to the subject, "the bar-tailed godwit." No other punctuation belongs between that subject and its verb, "doubles."

B.why: You left the introductory material unclosed. With no comma, "satellite tracking the bar-tailed godwit" reads as if the tracking acts on the bird, and the sentence loses its subject.

C.why: You added a comma after the subject. The comma after "tracking" already closes the introductory material, so the comma after "godwit" wrongly separates the subject from its verb, "doubles."

D.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. Everything before it is an introductory phrase with no subject or main verb, so it's a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In a twelve-week study of competitive rowers, the researchers' primary outcome, the athletes' lactate threshold (the exercise intensity at which lactate accumulates in the blood faster than the body can clear ______ by an average of 7 percent. Rowers who had done most of their training at lower intensities showed the largest gains.
explanation: Two interruptions are nested here. The parenthesis closes the definition of "lactate threshold." The comma after "outcome" opened the appositive "the athletes' lactate threshold (...)," and that appositive still needs its own closing comma before the main verb "rose." With everything removed, you get "the researchers' primary outcome rose by an average of 7 percent."

A.why: You closed the parenthesis but forgot the comma that opened the appositive after "outcome." Closing the inner interruption doesn't close the outer one.

B.why: You closed the appositive with a different mark than the one that opened it. It began with a comma after "outcome," so it has to end with a comma, not a dash.

D.why: You added "and" as if two verbs were being joined. "Outcome" has no verb before "rose," so "and" has nothing to join, and the sentence loses its main verb.
